name: Voice agents
h1: Text to speech for voice agents and phone bots
metaDescription: How a voice agent turns each reply into speech with a streaming text-to-speech API: the steps, a sample reply, when to choose ReadAloud and what to check first.
intro: A voice agent listens to a caller, decides what to say, and speaks the answer. The speaking step is text to speech, and for a live conversation two things matter more than they do for a recorded narration: how soon the first sound arrives after the reply is ready, and whether the speech can be cut off the moment the caller interrupts. ReadAloud Live is the low-latency tier built for this job. It streams audio over a WebSocket or over HTTP, so your agent can start playing the first sentence while the language model is still writing the rest, and a stop message ends the current speech at once. This page walks through how that fits into an agent, shows a sample reply as text, and lists the cases where another service is a better fit, for example when you need many voices or languages. It makes no claim about how the audio sounds. Try it on your own replies with the free credits before you decide, and measure the time to first audio from your own servers, because results depend on where you run.
steps: Get an API key and keep it on your server, not in a browser or phone app.
Authorize a connection for ReadAloud Live and open the WebSocket, keeping it open across replies.
Send each reply as a synthesize message as soon as the first sentence is ready, instead of waiting for the full answer.
Play the audio chunks as they arrive, using the format your phone line or player expects.
Send a stop message when the caller interrupts, and start the next reply when your agent has one.

sampleExample.title: A reply a booking agent might speak
sampleExample.input: Thanks for calling Riverside Dental. I can offer you Tuesday at ten thirty or Thursday at two. Which one works better for you?
sampleExample.notes: About 120 characters, well inside the 5,000-character limit for one request. Split longer replies at sentence boundaries.

whenToChooseReadAloud: You want low-priced streaming speech in English for a live agent.
You use Pipecat or LiveKit Agents and want a plugin that handles interruption.
You want to try an OpenAI-compatible endpoint by changing a base URL.
whenToChooseSomethingElse: You need many voices, accents or languages other than English.
You rely on SSML for pauses and pronunciation.
You need a certification that ReadAloud does not claim.

featuresUsed.howItHelps: The low-latency tier streams audio as sentences are ready.
One open connection carries many replies.
8 kHz mu-law and A-law output suit phone lines.

considerations: Measure time to first audio from your own servers with your own replies.
Plan for a retry with a short backoff if the service reports it is at capacity.

faq.q: Can I stop speech when the caller interrupts?
faq.a: Yes. A stop message ends the current speech at once, and only requests that finish are billed.

faq.q: Which tier should a voice agent use?
faq.a: ReadAloud Live is the tier built for live calls. ReadAloud Studio is the higher-priced tier with several English voices.

faq.q: Does it support phone audio formats?
faq.a: The WebSocket route can return 8 kHz mu-law and A-law audio for phone lines.

faq.q: What does it cost to test?
faq.a: Every account gets a one-time grant of free credits worth about 10,000 characters of speech.
